summary: For ages 10-11, this is the capstone of 'look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning': abstract a general algebraic rule from a run of specific cases AND verify it on a fresh case. Learners build the interior-angle-sum rule (n−2)×180° from triangle/quadrilateral/pentagon, write the nth-term rule of a linear sequence to predict any term, and generalise structural facts about operations — each time testing the generalisation on a specific case. The core discrimination is twofold: (a) capturing the −2 offset / start value instead of assuming direct proportion (n×180°, or 20th term = 20×first term), and (b) treating verification on a new case as a reflex, not an afterthought. Teaching should tabulate the cases so the constant step and offset are visible, press for the rule in words then symbols, decompose the geometric case so the rule is explained rather than curve-fitted, and always demand a verifying case.
misconceptions: Uses a term-to-term rule and cannot produce an nth-term rule for a far term
Assumes direct proportion — e.g. angle sum is n×180° or the 20th term is 20×(first term) — ignoring the −2 offset / start value
States a generalisation but never verifies it on a specific case, so errors go uncaught
Fits a rule to the given cases that fails to generalise (a pattern that works for 3, 4, 5 sides but wasn't reasoned from structure)

activities.title: Polygon angle-sum explorer: build, tabulate, abstract, verify
steps: Start with a triangle (angle sum 180°). Add one side at a time to make a quadrilateral, then a pentagon (convex shapes); for each, split the polygon into triangles by drawing diagonals from one vertex. Keep the hexagon back as a fresh test case.
Record in a running table: number of sides, number of triangles, and angle sum. Notice the sum climbs by a steady +180° each time while the triangle count stays at (sides − 2).

Explain WHY: in a convex polygon, from one vertex you can reach the n−3 non-adjacent vertices by diagonals, so an n-sided polygon splits into exactly n−2 triangles, and its angle sum is (n−2) lots of 180° — reason the rule from the structure, don't just fit it to the numbers.
Write the general rule in words ('two fewer than the number of sides, times 180°') then in symbols: (n−2)×180°.

Verify on a case you did not build the rule from: test a hexagon — (6−2)×180° = 720° — and check it matches the measured/added angles. Then stretch it: a decagon (10 sides, 1440°) and a 100-gon — does it still make sense?
activities.insight: The angle sum is (n−2)×180° BECAUSE the polygon decomposes into n−2 triangles — a rule explained by structure, and confirmed by testing a new polygon rather than trusted on faith.

activities.title: nth-term rule tester for a linear sequence
steps: Take a linear sequence such as 5, 9, 13, 17, … and tabulate position (1, 2, 3, 4) against term so the constant difference (+4) and the start value are visible.
Move from the term-to-term rule ('add 4') to a position-to-term rule: difference × n + offset. For 5, 9, 13, 17 this is 4n + 1.
Predict a far term you cannot easily count to — the 20th term (81) and the 100th term (401) — using the rule, not step-by-step continuation.

Verify: first check your rule reproduces every listed term (e.g. the 4th term should give 4×4+1 = 17), then test a fresh case not used to build it — extend the sequence by one step to get the 5th term (21) and check that 4×5+1 = 21. If a conjectured rule breaks any term, it is wrong — fix it.
Explain why direct proportion fails here: the 20th term is NOT 20 × the first term, because the sequence does not pass through zero at position zero (the rule 4n+1 gives 1 at n=0, not 0).
activities.insight: A general nth-term rule lets you jump to any term directly, and the offset (start value) matters — direct proportion from the first term is a classic error that verification against a known term catches.

activities.title: Generalise a structural fact and find the case that disproves a false rule
steps: Generalise an operation property with a reason, e.g. 'any whole number m divided by a non-zero whole number n can be written as the fraction m/n, so dividing by n gives a denominator of n (before any simplifying)' — state it, then justify why it holds, not just that it works on examples.

Explore the cancelling regularity in products like (x−1)(x+1), (x−1)(x²+x+1), … and describe the general pattern that emerges; an area model or algebra tiles may help visualise the simpler binomial product (x−1)(x+1), but are harder to apply to the cubic case, so treat them as an optional aid rather than a required method.

Practise verification-by-counterexample: given a false claim such as 'a polygon's angle sum is n×180°', name the specific polygon that shows it is wrong and state what it gives versus the true value (e.g. pentagon: rule gives 900°, truth is 540°).
Answer the discriminating prompt: 'Why n−2 and not n — what does the −2 correspond to in the shape?'
activities.insight: Generalising means stating a rule, justifying why it holds from structure, and being able to produce the single case that would disprove a false version — all three are part of mathematical reasoning.

checkQuestion: A triangle's angles add to 180°, a quadrilateral's to 360°, a pentagon's to 540°. What is the rule for the angle sum of a polygon with n sides? How did you get it — and test your rule on a hexagon.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for (n−2)×180° reached by reasoning (each extra side adds 180° / an n-gon is n−2 triangles), and a verification on the hexagon giving (6−2)×180 = 720°. The reasoned rule AND the check are the target, not the formula alone.
